title: Program versus process
story:
A program is a file. It is bytes at rest, no more active than a recipe card, and it stays exactly as inert whether it is run once, a thousand times, or never. A process is what exists while those bytes are being executed, and almost everything interesting about running software is a property of the second rather than the first.

Starting one is a sequence of allocations performed by the kernel. It reads the file's header to learn how the contents should be arranged in memory, then maps that content into a fresh private address space. It sets aside a region for the chain of function calls and their local values, and another that the program can grow at will as it asks for more memory. It builds a table of the open channels the program can read and write, with the standard input, output and error streams already in place. Then it hands control to a thread of execution with its own register state and a pointer to the next instruction to run.

The private address space is the part that earns its keep, and the reason is worth following. The addresses a program uses are not the addresses the hardware uses. A translation layer in the processor maps one to the other, and each process gets its own map — so two instances of the same program, executing the same instructions on the same machine, address what looks like the same location and reach different physical memory. That is why running a program twice does not corrupt either copy, and it is not a convention the programs cooperate in. It is enforced below them, by hardware they cannot reach around.

Which explains, in one move, something that otherwise looks like an arbitrary restriction: why processes cannot simply share variables. There is no shared naming scheme to share them through. An address means something only relative to one map, so a pointer handed to another process refers to whatever happens to live at that address under its map — which is why passing data between processes needs an explicit channel the kernel provides, whether a pipe, a local socket, or a region both sides have deliberately asked to have mapped into both address spaces.

Keeping the distinction straight also settles a class of confusion that has nothing to do with memory. A file being present is not a program running. A program being correct is not a process behaving, because a process also has an environment, a working directory, an identity, open channels and a parent — none of which are in the file. Two processes from one file can differ in every one of those and behave completely differently while executing identical instructions. So when the same binary works in one place and not another, the difference is by definition not in the program.

problem.name: The file is not the execution
problem.shape: Something about running software needs explaining, and the explanation is being sought in the file.
tell: the same binary behaves differently in two places
two copies are expected to interfere and do not, or are expected not to and do
a design assumes two processes can share a variable
a correctness argument is made about the file rather than the execution
problem.move: Separate what is in the file from what the kernel supplies at start-up: the address space, the open channels, the working directory, the environment, the identity, the parent. When behaviour differs between two runs of the same file, the difference is in that second list by elimination.
problem.invariant: A program is inert content; a process is content plus the context the kernel gives it. Identical instructions in different contexts are different executions.
problem.breaks: The isolation is per-process, and threads inside one process deliberately do not have it — they share the address space by design, which is the whole reason they are cheap and the whole reason they are dangerous. So 'each execution is isolated' is true at the wrong granularity for most concurrent code.

cost.time: translation on memory accesses, and the kernel work of building an address space on every start
cost.space: per-process page tables and duplicated mappings, which is why a process is expensive relative to a thread
cost.beats: running without isolation, which is faster and lets one stray write take down everything, and putting all the work in threads of one process, which is cheap and gives up the protection entirely

worked.problem: Why can two copies of the same program run at once without corrupting each other, and why can they not simply share a variable?
worked.reasoning:
Both answers are the same fact seen from two sides: each process gets its own map from the addresses it uses to the memory that actually exists.

Start with what the kernel does at start-up, because the isolation is built there rather than being a property of the file. It reads the header to learn how the contents should be laid out, maps that content into a fresh private address space, sets aside a region for the call chain and its local values and another the program can grow on demand, builds a table of open channels with the standard streams in place, and hands control to a thread with its own registers and a pointer to the next instruction.

The private address space is the answer to the first half. The addresses a program uses are not the addresses the hardware uses — a translation layer in the processor maps between them, and each process has its own map. So two instances executing the same instruction, referring to what is textually the same location, reach different physical memory. Nothing in either program is aware of this and neither has to cooperate: it is enforced underneath them by hardware they cannot reach around, which is what makes it a guarantee rather than a convention.

The second half follows immediately, and this is the part I would emphasise because it converts an apparently arbitrary restriction into a consequence. There is no shared naming scheme through which a variable could be shared. An address is meaningful only relative to one map, so handing a pointer to another process names whatever happens to sit at that address under its map — which is not the same object and is not even reliably anything. That is why passing data between processes requires a channel the kernel provides: a pipe, a local socket, or a region both sides have explicitly asked to have mapped into both address spaces. The last one is interesting because it is the exception that proves the rule — shared memory works precisely by arranging, deliberately and with the kernel's participation, for two maps to agree.

There is a broader use for the distinction that has nothing to do with memory. A process has an environment, a working directory, an identity, open channels and a parent, none of which are in the file. Two processes started from one file can differ in all of them and behave completely differently while executing identical instructions. So when the same binary works in one place and not another, the difference is by elimination not in the program — which turns 'it works on my machine' from a mystery into a finite list of things to compare.

One correction to the general claim, because it is stated too broadly more often than not. The isolation is per-process, and threads within a single process deliberately do not have it: they share one address space, which is exactly why they are cheap to create and exactly why data races are possible at all. So 'every execution is isolated from every other' is true at a granularity most concurrent code does not operate at.

problem.practice: Start the same program twice and compare everything the kernel gave each copy rather than anything in the file: working directory, environment, open channels, identity, parent. That list is where every 'works on my machine' lives.

beats.broke: Executions ran without isolation, so one stray write or one runaway loop in any program could take down the whole machine, and no program could be reasoned about independently of every other.
beats.fix: Give each execution its own map from the addresses it uses to the memory that exists, enforced by the processor, so identical instructions in two processes reach different physical memory without either program cooperating.
beats.cost: Translation on every access and a fresh address space per start-up, which is why a process is expensive next to a thread — and why the cheap alternative gives the protection back up.

interview.q: Why can two copies of the same program run at once without corrupting each other, and why can they not simply share a variable?
interview.trap: Explaining the isolation as something the programs or the language arrange. It is enforced below them by address translation, which is why it is a guarantee rather than a convention — and why the sharing restriction is a consequence rather than a policy.
interview.answer:
Both are the same fact from two sides: each process has its own map from the addresses it uses to the memory that actually exists.

The isolation is built at start-up rather than living in the file. The kernel reads the header to learn the layout, maps the content into a fresh private address space, sets aside a region for the call chain and one the program can grow on demand, builds a table of open channels with the standard streams in place, and hands control to a thread with its own registers and a pointer to the next instruction.

That private address space answers the first half. The addresses a program uses are not the hardware's addresses; a translation layer in the processor maps between them and each process has its own map, so two instances executing the same instruction on what is textually the same location reach different physical memory. Neither program knows or has to cooperate — it is enforced underneath them by hardware they cannot reach around, which is what makes it a guarantee.

The second half follows, and it turns an apparently arbitrary restriction into a consequence: there is no shared naming scheme through which to share a variable. An address is meaningful only relative to one map, so a pointer handed to another process names whatever sits there under its map — not the same object, not reliably anything. Hence explicit channels: a pipe, a local socket, or a region both sides have asked to have mapped into both spaces. That last is the exception proving the rule, since shared memory works by deliberately arranging for two maps to agree.

The distinction earns its keep elsewhere too. A process has an environment, working directory, identity, open channels and a parent, none of which are in the file — so two processes from one file can behave completely differently while executing identical instructions, which turns 'it works on my machine' into a finite list to compare.

One correction, since this gets stated too broadly: the isolation is per process. Threads inside one process deliberately share an address space, which is exactly why they are cheap and exactly why data races exist at all.

takeaway: A program is inert content and a process is that content plus the address space, channels and identity the kernel gives it — so two copies cannot collide because each has its own map from names to memory, cannot share a variable for exactly the same reason, and any difference between two runs of one binary is by elimination outside the file.
